constrained_activity: sequencing and clinically interpreting an individual human genome

historical_constraint.statement: Whole-genome sequencing cost ~$95M per genome as of 2001, restricting it to large centralized projects.

historical_evidence.citation: NHGRI / genome.gov, DNA Sequencing Costs Data

change_driver.statement: Next-generation (massively parallel) sequencing platforms replaced Sanger capillary sequencing starting ~2007-2008.

current_evidence.citation: genome.gov / Our World in Data, cost-of-sequencing-a-full-human-genome
Genetics in Medicine (2021), 'Challenges in genetic testing: clinician variant interpretation processes and the impact on clinical care'
current_evidence.value: bottleneck explicitly stated to have moved to variant interpretation

replacement_constraint.statement: Clinical variant interpretation capacity, not sequencing throughput, is the current binding constraint on turning a genome into a diagnosis.

provenance: Genetics in Medicine (2021), 'Challenges in genetic testing: clinician variant interpretation processes and the impact on clinical care'

constrained_activity: placing a long-distance or international voice call

historical_constraint.statement: A 3-minute transatlantic call cost ~$12 in 1950 under a regulated monopoly carrier structure.

change_driver.statement: Transatlantic submarine cable deployment cut the same call to ~$3 in the 1960s, ~$1.70 by 1968; AT&T Bell System breakup (1984) opened long-distance to competition, cutting prices further; fiber-optic capacity compounded this through the 1980s-90s.

change_evidence.citation: KiowaCountyPress / Click Americana, historical long-distance pricing
Search-summarized reporting on 1984 AT&T breakup price effect

current_evidence.value: 31% of US adults report >=1 scam call/day

replacement_constraint.statement: Near-zero call-initiation cost enabled scam/robocall volume at a scale that makes caller verification, not connection cost, the binding constraint on a call's value.

provenance: KiowaCountyPress / Click Americana, historical long-distance pricing
Search-summarized reporting on 1984 AT&T breakup price effect
unresolved_questions: No citation found in this pass for the pre-cable-era organizational adaptation to expensive calling (telex/mail substitution, centralized switchboards) - plausible, not confirmed.

constrained_activity: opening a bank branch outside the bank's home state

historical_constraint.statement: McFadden Act (1927), extended by the Douglas Amendment (1956), confined national banks and bank holding companies to branching within their home state.

historical_adaptation.statement: States adopted reciprocal interstate agreements from the early 1980s (46 states by 1990), letting bank holding companies acquire out-of-state banks years before the federal restriction was lifted.

change_driver.statement: Riegle-Neal Interstate Banking and Branching Efficiency Act of 1994 removed the federal interstate branching restriction.

change_evidence.citation: Federal Reserve History, 'Riegle-Neal Interstate Banking and Branching Efficiency Act of 1994'

current_evidence.citation: Riegle-Neal Act text, deposit concentration provisions
current_evidence.note: The cap itself is the current binding rule, still in force as enacted; this pass did not verify subsequent amendment history.

regulatory_burden.now_value: branching permitted, subject to 10%/30% deposit concentration cap

replacement_constraint.statement: A deposit-concentration cap (10% national / 30% state) replaces the geographic branching prohibition as the binding regulatory limit on large-bank expansion.

provenance: Federal Reserve History, 'Riegle-Neal Interstate Banking and Branching Efficiency Act of 1994'
Riegle-Neal Act text, deposit concentration provisions
unresolved_questions: Has the 10%/30% cap itself been amended or waived since 1994? Not checked in this pass.
How binding is the concentration cap in practice today - has any institution approached it? Not checked.

constrained_activity: manufacturing and deploying a photovoltaic power system

historical_constraint.statement: Solar PV modules cost ~$106/watt (inflation-adjusted) in 1976, restricting deployment to niche non-grid applications.

historical_evidence.citation: Our World in Data / Voronoi, citing Nemet (2009)

change_driver.statement: ~20% module price decline per doubling of cumulative installed capacity (learning curve), driven by manufacturing scale-up and large deployment programs.

change_evidence.citation: Our World in Data, solar-pv-prices-vs-cumulative-capacity, citing Nemet (2009) and Farmer & Lafond (2016)

current_evidence.value: soft costs = 50% of $3.25/W median installed cost ($1.64/W); panels ~13%, BOS/inverters ~33%, office work alone ~26%

replacement_constraint.statement: Installation, permitting, and customer-acquisition ('soft') costs now account for 45-60% of total residential system cost and are cited by NREL as the largest, most persistent contributor to solar pricing -- the module cost constraint weakened while the labor/coordination constraint around deploying it did not fall at a comparable rate.

provenance: Our World in Data / Voronoi, citing Nemet (2009)
Our World in Data, solar-pv-prices-vs-cumulative-capacity, citing Nemet (2009) and Farmer & Lafond (2016)
